extracted.intended_audience: newspaper reporters and journalism students (society editors/writers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for reporting and writing social and personal (society) news—how to select, phrase, format, and place items such as courtships, engagements, weddings, reunions, and social functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public interest justifies dedicated society department
rubrics_metrics.description: Interest in social and personal news is so great that practically every newspaper maintains a society department under the direction of a society editor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that society items attract strong reader interest; organize coverage (and staffing) accordingly rather than treating such items as minor copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt form and style to social usage
rubrics_metrics.description: The form and style suitable to such news are partly determined by social usage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let contemporary social conventions guide tone, emphasis, and what details are appropriate to include or omit for a given audience or class of event.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typographical style may differ from other parts of the paper
rubrics_metrics.description: The typographical style of the society columns often differs somewhat from that of other parts of the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of and follow the paper's typographical conventions for society pages (headlines, names, datelines, dress/flower descriptions) to meet reader expectations and ease reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide variety for repetitive events
rubrics_metrics.description: Society news taxes the writer's ability to give variety to stories of the same kind of events as they take place day by day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid monotonous repetition—seek fresh angles, new details, or different narrative emphases when reporting engagements, weddings, and receptions that recur frequently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid stock phrases and trite, colorless description
rubrics_metrics.description: In no other kind of news is he more frequently tempted to use stock phrases over and over again. It is possible, however, to give considerable variety to society stories as well as to avoid trite, colorless, description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actively weed out clichés and stock wording. Vary sentence openings, descriptive language, and detail selection; editing should remove patent phrases that make copy dull.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat unusual courtships/engagements/weddings as regular news when warranted
rubrics_metrics.description: Unusual courtships, engagements, and weddings may be treated as regular news; in that case the stories of them are not often placed in the society section.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an item has broader public-news value (oddity, public-interest angle, legal/financial implications), give it full news treatment and consider placement outside the society column.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop humorous or pathetic possibilities without violating good taste
rubrics_metrics.description: Such news not infrequently has humorous and pathetic possibilities that the writer may develop without violating the canons of good taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When emphasizing human-interest, humor, or pathos, do so sensitively—avoid sensationalism, ridicule, or invasions of privacy; keep tone respectful and within standards of taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include conventional social-detail elements (implicit standard from examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Society items commonly record specific details: names of bride/bridegroom and parents, officiant, description of dress and flowers, attendants, reception location, and notable guests or family background.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these conventional elements as a checklist when composing short society items; include salient biographical or social affiliations that matter to readers, but trim superfluous minutiae.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use illustrative anecdotes and concrete incidents to enliven copy
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples in the chapter (unusual courtship, hero-rescues-bride, cowboy wedding, elopement, septuagenarian romance) illustrate that concrete anecdotes and striking incidents make society copy engaging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lead with a memorable detail or anecdote when available (a novena leading to a marriage, a rescue that led to romance, an eccentric wedding procession) to hook readers and distinguish the story from routine items.
